messages.subject: Re: renin-script-engine - java class inheritance
messages.body_plain:
Hi Julien,
There is a very basic version of this implemented as part of ScriptEngine interface. Here is an example of implementing java.lang.Runnable:

RenjinScriptEngine engine;
engine.eval("run <- function() print('Running!')");

Runnable runnable = engine.getInterface(Runnable.class);
runnable.run();
// prints "Running"

If you look at the implementation of RenjinScriptEngine.getInterface(), you might roll your own version that calls methods in a list or passes an object as a first argument:
https://github.com/bedatadriven/renjin/blob/master/script-engine/src/main/java/org/renjin/script/RenjinScriptEngine.java#L197-197

Hope this helps!

Alex

messages.subject: Re: Compiling from Source Question
messages.body_plain:
Hi Kevin,
You can find binaries (without dependencies) for all Renjin artifacts
and releases here:
https://nexus.bedatadriven.com/content/groups/public/org/renjin/

If you have a maven/gradle/ivy/sbt/ build etc, you should just be able
to include renjin-script-engine in your build:

<dependency>
<groupId>org.renjin</groupId>
<artifactId>renjin-script-engine</artifactId>
<version>RELEASE</version>
</dependency>

Depending on your build tool, you should be able to excerise some
control over transitive dependency conflict resolution such as Guava,
though Renjin won't run against earlier versions of Guava.

We have an open request to repackage Guava in Renjin's namespace to
avoid these problems:
https://github.com/bedatadriven/renjin/issues/63

I'll also take a look at the Vagrant setup to see why the build is
failing there...

Alex

messages.subject: Re: SVM (e1071) from Java
messages.body_plain:
Hi Joël,
It looks like e1071 has C++ code which our toolchain does not yet compile. (Issue #119 <https://github.com/bedatadriven/renjin/issues/119>)

The message you're seeing is only a warning because the Java class that will eventually contain the compiled C/C++ code is missing.

If there are functions in e1071 that don't rely on the C/C++ code, then they should work fine, but unfortunately any functions which rely on C/C++ for this package will fail.

We're making good progress on the native code compiler, but unfortunatley for this package at least, we're not there yet.

Alex

messages.subject: Calling Ruby method from Renjin
messages.body_plain:
Hi all….,

I thought you could find it interesting that I was able to call a Ruby method from Renjin, in a similar way that you call a Java method from Renjin.

The details:

I have implemented the following interface in Java:
public interface RubyCallbackInterface {

    public Object run();
    public Object run(Object obj1);
    public Object run(Object obj1, Object obj2);
    public Object run(Object obj1, Object obj2, Object obj3);
    public Object run(Object obj1, Object obj2, Object obj3, Object obj4);
    public Object run(Object obj1, Object obj2, Object obj3, Object obj4, Object obj5);
    public Object run(Object obj1, Object obj2, Object obj3, Object obj4, Object obj5, Object obj6);
    public Object run(Object obj1, Object obj2, Object obj3, Object obj4, Object obj5, Object obj6, Object obj7);

}

I´ve implemented it like this because doing public Object run(Object… ) Renjin says there is no method that matches my run interface when I call it. Seems to me like a bug. But for now this is working fine.

Then on the Ruby side I implement a class that implements this interface like so:
class Callback < Renjin::RubySexp
  include Java::RbScicom.RubyCallbackInterface

  attr_reader :ruby_obj

  def initialize(ruby_obj)
    @ruby_obj = ruby_obj
  end

  def run(*args)
    method = args[0]
    args.shift
    @ruby_obj.send(method, *args)
  end

  def self.pack(obj, recursive: false)

    if recursive
      container = Array.new
      obj.each do |pk|
        container << Callback.new(pk)
      end
      container
    else
      Callback.new(obj)
    end

  end

end

Basically what this code does, is create a class that has a ‘run’ method that receives a ‘name’ and a ‘list of arguments’. The ‘name’ is the method name to be called and the argument list are the arguments to send to the method if it requires any.  The pack method can either pack a class or pack the content of the class if we have a container.

This works fine. So, lets now try it:
  # create two Ruby arrays, props1 and props2
  props1 = [1, 2, 3]
  props2 = [1, 2]

  # add the two  Ruby arrays into another Ruby array
  props = [props1, props2]

  # Now we 'pack' our arrays inside a Callback class so that we can call method run on them from R
  cb = R.rpack(props, recursive: true)

  # Now we write an R script that call method.  #{cb.r} converts the cb Ruby variable to an R variable
  R.eval("val <- sapply(#{cb.r}, function(x) x$run('length'))")
  R.eval("print(val)")

This returns:
  [1] 3 2

This is really amazing!!!
​
--
Rodrigo Botafogo
